qt: to the Commission Dolors Montserrat (PPE) Subject:

The ‘Bolaños Law’ in Spain has done away with the automatic granting of legal aid to child victims of certain serious non-sexual crimes, instead forcing them to prove they cannot afford legal assistance. The Spanish Public Prosecutor’s Office has warned that this new arrangement may lead to people being left without assistance and has called for protection to be restored. In the light of Directive 2012/29/EU, which requires the best interests of the child to be a primary consideration and guarantees victims access to legal aid under the conditions established in national law: 1.
Does the Commission consider it compatible with EU law for child victims of serious crime to be left without specialised legal assistance if it cannot be proved that they cannot afford it themselves?
Has the Commission assessed whether this reform really protects the child’s best interests and prevents unjustified differences in how child victims are protected depending on the crime?

Does the Commission intend to request information from the Spanish authorities or take any action to ensure that Spanish legislation is fully consistent with the obligations arising from Directive 2012/29/EU?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (30.10.2026) The Victims’ Rights Directive1 provides that, where the victim is a child, the child’s best interests must be a primary consideration and must be assessed on an individual basis. While the Directive contains specific provisions on the right to legal aid, it does not provide for unconditional access to such a right. The revised Victims’ Rights Directive2, adopted in June 2026, further strengthens the right to legal aid by requiring that it be granted to specific categories of victims, including child victims, where they become parties to criminal proceedings and do not have sufficient means. However, the conditions and procedural rules on access to legal aid remain to be determined by national law, provided that national rules comply with the Directive’s requirements. Member States must transpose the revised Victims’ Rights Directive by 2 July 2028. After the deadline, the Commission will promptly assess whether the Directive has been correctly and fully transposed in all Member States, including Spain.
1 Directive 2012/29/EU of the European Parliament and of the Council of 25 October 2012 establishing

minimum standards on the rights, support and protection of victims of crime, and replacing Council Framework Decision 2001/220/JHA. 2 Article 13 of Directive (EU) 2026/1472 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 17 June 2026 amending Directive 2012/29/EU establishing minimum standards on the rights, support and protection of victims of crime, and replacing Council Framework Decision 2001/220/JHA.
